title: AI Diet Plans Look Convincing but Miss the Mark on Calories and Nutrition
excerpt: New research reveals AI-generated meal plans undercount calories by nearly 700 per day, while photo-based tracking apps miss up to 345 calories per meal.
body:
• AI-generated meal plans underestimate daily calorie needs by nearly 700 calories — the equivalent of skipping an entire meal — according to a study published in Frontiers in Nutrition.
  • Photo-based calorie tracking apps including MyFitnessPal and Lose It! underestimate calories by 250 to 345 per meal and fat by about 30 grams, NIH researchers found.
  • AI models consistently skew toward high-protein, low-carb patterns regardless of a user's age or medical needs, deviating significantly from clinical nutritional guidelines.
  • Experts warn against relying solely on AI for dietary decisions, particularly for teenagers, people with chronic conditions, or those following culturally specific diets.

The 700-Calorie Gap

When researchers at Istanbul Atlas University asked five popular AI chatbots — including ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Claude 4.1 — to create three-day meal plans for overweight teenagers, the results were alarming. On average, the AI-generated plans contained nearly 700 fewer calories per day than plans designed by a registered dietitian, according to findings published in Frontiers in Nutrition.

The gap is roughly equivalent to missing an entire meal. But the problem extended beyond simple undercounting. The AI models consistently pushed protein to 21 to 24 percent of total energy intake while inflating fat to 41 to 45 percent. Carbohydrates, meanwhile, were slashed to just 32 to 36 percent — well below the 45 to 50 percent recommended by the U.S. National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine.

"AI-generated diet plans consistently deviated from the recommended macronutrient balance, which is particularly problematic for adolescents," said Dr. Ayse Betul Bilen, an assistant professor at Istanbul Atlas University who led the study. "Following such unbalanced or overly restrictive meal plans during the teenage years may negatively affect growth, metabolic health, and eating behaviors."

"AI models are primarily trained to generate responses that appear plausible and user-friendly rather than clinically precise. They may rely on generalized or popular diet patterns instead of fully integrating age-specific nutritional requirements."

— Dr. Ayse Betul Bilen, Istanbul Atlas University

Photo-Based Apps Fare No Better

A separate study from the U.S. National Institutes of Health, presented at NUTRITION 2026 in July, tested a different promise of AI nutrition technology: snap a photo of your meal and get an instant calorie count.

NIH researchers photographed 102 meals prepared in a tightly controlled metabolic kitchen where every ingredient was precisely weighed. They then ran the images through four popular apps — MyFitnessPal, Lose It!, Cal AI, and Appediet. All four underestimated calorie content by 250 to 345 calories per meal and fat by approximately 30 grams, according to Aaron Hengist, a postdoctoral fellow at the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases.

"People using a photo-based tracking app without adjusting the portions or entering the amounts of food should take the results with a grain of salt," Hengist said. "These apps tend to underestimate calories, especially from fats, so what they actually ate is likely higher than what the app shows."

A follow-up analysis of more than 200 additional meals found the apps were particularly inaccurate with low-carb ketogenic meals, likely because they consistently underestimated the higher fat content in those dishes.

Why AI Gets Nutrition Wrong

The fundamental issue, researchers say, is that large language models are optimized to produce coherent, plausible-sounding output — not clinically precise recommendations. They draw from generalized dietary patterns popular online, which tend to skew toward trendy high-protein, low-carb approaches rather than established clinical guidelines.

This design characteristic is not a bug that will be fixed with the next software update. AI models do not consult nutritional databases or clinical guidelines the way a trained dietitian does. The resulting plans look professional enough to inspire confidence, which may be precisely the problem.

For the nearly two in three U.S. teenagers who report using AI chatbots, according to survey data, this poses real risks. And the concern extends to adults managing chronic conditions, where inaccurate dietary guidance could interfere with medical treatment.

What This Means for Indian Diets

The limitations carry additional implications for South Asian diets. AI models trained predominantly on Western food databases may poorly estimate calories in Indian cuisine, where cooking methods involve generous use of ghee, cooking oils, and complex spice preparations that significantly alter caloric density. Dishes like biryani, dal tadka, or paratha can vary widely in calorie content based on regional preparation methods — nuances that AI image recognition and meal planning tools are unlikely to capture.

Dietitians familiar with Indian cuisine also note that many traditional meals do not map neatly to the macronutrient ratios AI models tend to favor. A typical South Indian thali, for instance, derives a higher proportion of calories from rice and lentils than AI tools trained on Western dietary norms might recommend.

The Expert Consensus

Researchers from both studies converge on the same recommendation: AI tools can be useful starting points, but they should not replace professional dietary guidance. Combining AI-based tracking with traditional food logging methods and periodic consultation with a registered dietitian offers a more reliable path to accurate nutritional management.

For anyone using these tools to manage weight or a health condition, the takeaway is straightforward — trust the app's convenience, but verify its numbers.
